newsitem.title: USA: Santee Cooper looks to maintain power despite Fran.
newsitem.headline: Santee Cooper looks to maintain power despite Fran.

text.p: Santee Cooper, a South Carolina state-owned utility lying directly in the path of Hurricane Fran, said it expects to provide normal electricity service this week despite the storm.

"The only thing that is going to shut us down is if some of our (transmission) lines come down," company spokesman Jerry Stafford said Thursday. He said the company's coal-fired plants "are about as solid as anything out there."
Santee Cooper directly supplies power to about 106,000 retail and 30 industrial customers in the three coastal counties expected to be hit by Fran.
It also supplies power to distribution companies covering about two-thirds of the state, with total estimated customers of over one million people, Stafford said.
Meteorologists were warning Hurricane Fran will likely come ashore near Myrtle Beach, S.C.
Santee Cooper was forced to cut power in September, 1989, when Hurricane Hugo destryed several transmission lines and flying debris damaged one of its power production facilities.
But Stafford said Hurricane Hugo helped the company prepare for large storms.
"The big advantage is that Hugo really came through and removed the weak links in our chain in terms of transmission," Stafford said.
Nearby Santee Cooper, Carolina Power & Light Co shut down its Brunswick nuclear power plant late Wednesday in preparation for the hurricane.
The Brunswick plant, at Southport on the North Carolina coast, is just to the north of Fran's forecast path. The plant is made up of two generating units with a combined capacity of 1,521 MW.
-- Chris Reese, New York Power Desk 212-859-1627
